newsitem.title: USA: Clinton vetoes disaster relief bill.
newsitem.headline: Clinton vetoes disaster relief bill.

text.p: President Clinton Monday vetoed an $8.6 billion emergency money bill providing disaster relief funds for 35 flood-stricken states because it included unrelated Republican policies he strongly opposed.

In his veto message, Clinton said Congress had loaded the measure with unacceptable provisions "despite the obvious and urgent need to speed critical relief" to people in the Dakotas, Minnesota, California and 31 other states that were ravaged by floods and other natural disasters.
North and South Dakota were especially hard-hit.

"The time has come to stop playing politics with the lives of Americans in need and to send me a clean bill that I can and will sign the moment in reaches my desk," Clinton said in announcing his refusal to sign the bill.

The bill provided $5.4 billion for disaster assistance, including $89 million for House Speaker Newt Gingrich's home state of Georgia and $24 million for Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott's state of Mississippi.

It also included $1.9 billion to pay for military operations in Bosnia and the Persian Gulf and $262 million for feeding poor women and their children, for education and for a new transportation system at Yosemite National Park. The rest of the money was earmarked for highway construction, veteran's benefits and other purposes.

One of the two Republican riders Clinton opposed would guarantee federal agencies funding at the 1997 level if the Republican-led Congress and the Democratic White House fail to agree on funding by the Oct. 1 start of the fiscal year.
The White House regards this as a backdoor strategem that would enable Republicans to prevail in spending disputes.

Another provision he refused to accept would block the use of sampling to try to get a better fix on traditionally undercounted minorities in the 2000 census. Since minorities tend to vote Democratic and congressional districts are drawn by population, this also has partisan implications.
Clinton also objected to language in the bill that he said would promote the paving of unimproved roads in sensitive areas of national parks.

"I urge Congress to remove these extraneous provisions and to send me a straightforward disaster relief bill that I can sign promptly so that we can help hard-hit American families and businesses as they struggle to rebuild," he said.

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton received the disaster relief bill from Congress at 1:50 p.m. EDT (1750 GMT) and vetoed it at 2:09 p.m. (1809 GMT). The measure was on its way back to Capitol Hill at 2:18 p.m. (1818 GMT)," he said.

Congress could overturn Clinton's veto by mustering a two-thirds majority in both the Senate and the House, but since the House failed to pass the bill by that big a margin the first time around a veto override seemed improbable.

"In all likelihood we don't have the votes to override the veto," said Sen. Don Nickles, an Oklahoma Republican. A motion by North Dakota Democrat Sen. Byron Dorgan to have the Senate pass an unincumbered bill by unanimous consent failed.

McCurry said the most objectionable provisions of the vetoed bill were both "identical in one respect -- they have no business being on this bill. They have to do with political issues that can be solved elsewhere."
Asked what was likely to happen to the bill, McCurry said: "I think eventually politics is going to yield to disaster relief for the individuals and communities who need it."
